sections.html:
• Scientific name: Turbo fluctuosa / Turbo fluctuosus
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Specific gravity: 1.023–1.025
  • Optimal KH: 8–16
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: herbivorous
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour: light brown, reddish-brown, greenish, or orange with whitish and dark brown mottling

When buying Mexican Turbo snails, look for small ones that appear healthy and are moving. Make sure the snail has no shell problems (broken or damaged).

The operculum (the trap-door used to close the shell opening) is a good way to see whether the snail is healthy and alive: it falls off as soon as the snail dies, and will not close properly if there is something wrong with the snail.
These snails are native to the Gulf of California off the coast of Mexico and range from Cedros Island, Baja California to Peru, including the Galapagos and Tres Marias Islands.

Mexican turbo snails are found most commonly attached to and under rocks or coral reefs (especially on dead corals where the growth of fresh algal vegetation is abundant) and within mud and sand substrate in the intertidal zone. They are also found in the crevices of reefs and boulders.

The optimum depth for this species is between 1 m and 30 m. Its preferred habitat is the moderately exposed coral reef shore.

Mexican Turbo snails need to be in an established tank with sufficient size and water volume to support their needs. The minimum recommended tank size is 40 litres. The bigger the tank the better.

If you are buying them for algae control, the rule of thumb is generally 1 Turbo snail per 20–40 litres. It depends on the conditions of your tank and how many algae you have. If the situation is totally out of control, or you want to remove algae as fast as possible, keeping 1 snail per 10 litres is recommended. Be conservative in stocking because their appetites are enormous. If there is no rush, Turbo snails will eventually deal with the problem, and if you have lots of them it will become problematic to feed them later.

The water should be 20–26°C, with 21–23°C being optimal. Alkalinity (KH) 8–12. Optimal pH is 8.1–8.4 and specific gravity is 1.023–1.025. Nitrate should be less than 20 ppm.

When the pH is lower than this range, shell growth can be disrupted and the snail's shell damaged.

They can tolerate most types of water movement but prefer slow-moving water.

Mexican Turbo snails do not tolerate high temperatures well in saltwater tanks, and they do not tolerate poor husbandry well. They are rather sensitive even to small changes in water values, so acclimate them carefully and very slowly, as with all invertebrates; 2–3 hours is generally good enough.

For the substrate, you can use either sand or small gravel. In the wild, Mexican Turbo snails usually prefer intertidal sandy-bottom substrates, so sand is the most ideal substrate for them. These snails are great at aerating the substrate as well.

Include plenty of live rock for the Turbo snails to graze on and use as hiding areas that help them feel secure.

They do not need fancy filtration and lighting. A normal LED aquarium light is enough.

Mexican turbo snails are herbivorous, mostly associated with specific food sources such as algae and seaweed. If you have problems with hair algae, slime (filamentous) algae, brown macroalgae, diatoms or cyanobacteria, these snails can help. They eat algae growing on aquarium glass, sand and rocks, which is why people use them to keep the glass clean for longer. You can see their tracks as they graze.

They can hold blades of soft algae between two halves of the front part of the foot, so they can pick up and eat algal fronds deposited on the bottom of an aquarium.

In aquariums, these snails will also feed on leftover shrimp or fish food, such as pills, flakes, pellets, algae/spirulina wafers, frozen foods, etc.

Important: Mexican turbo snails need a lot of food, so be prepared to supplement with herbivore pellets (algae pellets, dried algae, etc.) if there is not enough algae growth.

Be careful with copper: Mexican turbo snails are sensitive to copper and copper compounds.

Like all snails, they need calcium either in their diet or in the water (ideally both) to make their shells hard enough. Keeping calcium levels between 350 and 450 ppm is best. Calcium is vital for good shell growth.

Mexican turbo snails are very peaceful: if attacked by an aggressive hermit crab or fish, all they do is hunker down inside their shell.

They move extremely slowly but cover a large area while foraging. Younger snails are more active than older ones. Although not very shy, they appreciate having hiding places in the tank; in the wild they like to hide in holes and crevices.

They are nocturnal and start grazing after the lights are off. They also become active a few hours after being kept in darkness, regardless of the time of day.

When they fall upside-down they are generally able to right themselves, but because of their heavy shells this is not easy, so it is worth helping them. Being upside-down makes them vulnerable to predation from tankmates.

They are not burrowers and spend the vast majority of their time below the waterline, so the risk of escaping is pretty low.

Reef safe: yes. They will not damage anything in a reef tank on purpose and do not snack on corals. However, because of their size and strength they tend to knock things around, and many aquarists report that they bulldoze through corals. To prevent incidents, some aquarists advise gluing corals to the rocks.

Tankmates: They are good companions to shrimp and non-carnivorous fish. They are compatible with shrimp such as Sexy shrimp, Pederson cleaner shrimp, Red Fire shrimp (Lysmata debelius), Peppermint shrimp (Lysmata wurdemanni) or Skunk cleaner (Lysmata amboinensis), and with snails such as Bumble Bee snail, Fighting Conch snail, Cerith snails, Trochus snails, etc. Bumble Bee snails can attack weak or upside-down Mexican Turbo snails if there is not enough food in the tank.

Keeping them with Coral banded shrimp, crabs and hermit crabs is not advised, especially hermit crabs such as the Halloween hermit crab or Blue Leg hermit crab, which can try to kill them for their shells. If you still keep hermit crabs, make sure they have numerous empty shells spread through the tank; this can reduce aggression but will not eliminate it.
Mexican Turbo snails are gonochoric (separate male and female individuals) but cannot be distinguished externally. There is no official data on when and at what size they become sexually mature.

It is relatively difficult to breed Mexican Turbo snails in aquariums. Fertilization is external and nocturnal.

Spawning is initiated by males. Female spawning is induced in response to the presence of the male's sperm in the water. Females generally spawn for 5–10 minutes, releasing oocytes (unfertilized eggs) into the water column.

Although females can release a lot of eggs, the mortality rate is very high and only a few survive to become adults.

Mexican turbo snails have domed, spiral-shaped shells that typically grow up to 5 cm, though old snails can get larger than 7 cm. Colours vary: light brown, reddish-brown, greenish, or orange with whitish and dark brown mottling. The shells are thick and consist of five rounded whorls with angled shoulders.

The head has two small tentacles to help them find food and sense the environment. Their eyes are directly behind the tentacles and detect light and motion.

In nature, they can live 3–5 years, while in aquariums they often do not live more than 1.5 years.

They are excellent scavengers and algae eaters, mostly kept as part of a clean-up crew, but they can be hard to keep alive for a long time. They are not very hardy. Where small spaces are a problem, Cerith or Astrea snails can be added, as their small size lets them reach holes and crevices that turbo snails cannot.
